rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the basmala, ism is an added connective that shifts the phrase from the force of an oath to seeking blessing; the underlying wording is billāh.
rows.anchor: صلة زائدة، زيدت ليخرج بذكرها من حكم القسم الى قصد التبرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif is omitted in writing bism because the phrase is frequent and the prefixed bāʾ already supplies the linkage; it remains in bismi al-Raḥmān and similar phrases.
rows.anchor: من الخط تخفيفا لكثرة الاستعمال واستغناء عنها بباء الالصاق في اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial alif in ism is hamzat waṣl: the form sumayy shows that it is not pronounced and is dropped.
rows.anchor: وحذفت لانها ليست من اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamzat waṣl is supplied to let speech begin despite an initial sukūn, then becomes unnecessary when the word is joined to what precedes it.
rows.anchor: وانما زيدت لسكون الحرف الذي بعدها لما ارادوا استئنافه فلم يصلوا الى الابتداء بساكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same waṣl rule applies to initial alifs in verbs or verbal nouns whose imperfect form begins with a fatḥa vowel on its yāʾ, as in the cited imperatives.
rows.anchor: وكذلك كل الف كانت في اول فعل او مصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When these verb alifs begin speech they are normally pronounced with kasra; if the third letter is ḍamma, the initial vowel is ḍamma to ease the transition without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: مكسورات، فاذا استأنفت قلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An initial ḍamma is used when the verb's third letter is ḍamma because moving from kasra through a sukūn to ḍamma is difficult.
rows.anchor: الا ما كان منه ثالث حروفه مضموما فانك تضم أوله اذا استأنفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In words beginning with the added alif-lām, the alif drops in connected speech and is always fatḥa when starting; the two letters function together like qad or bal.
rows.anchor: كل اسم في أوله ألف ولام زائدتان فالالف تذهب اذا اتصلت بكلام قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif-lām is recognized as added because another alif-lām cannot be prefixed to words such as al-ḥamd, al-ʿālamīn, alladhī, and Allāh.
rows.anchor: لا تستطيع أن تدخل عليهن الفا ولاما أخريين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A preceding interrogative alif preserves and lengthens the article alif to distinguish a question from a statement; only a few Arabs leave it unlengthened.
rows.anchor: وانما مدت في الاستفهام ليفرق بين الاستفهام والخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With an interrogative alif before aṣṭafā or aftarā, the interrogative is open and the following hamzat waṣl drops.
rows.anchor: الالفات مفتوحة مقطوعة، لأنها ألف استفهام

rows.speaker: من قرأ هذه الآية
rows.claim: A reader cuts the alif of attakhadhnāhum as an interrogative.
rows.anchor: وقال من قرأ هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading joins attakhadhnāhum to the preceding context of am zāghat ʿanhum al-abṣār.
rows.anchor: وقد قرىء هذا الحرف موصولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An initial alif is hamzat qaṭʿ when another article can be added, as with al-ilāh, alwāḥ, ilhām, and ilqāʾ.
rows.anchor: فالالف من ذلك مقطوعة تكون في الاستئناف على حالها في الاتصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif in ilā is also cut, but it is not an added article: ilā is a preposition rather than a noun, and its alif is kasra rather than fatḥa.
rows.anchor: لأنها ليست باسم، وانما تدخل الالف واللام على الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamdu is nominative as a subject begun without a preceding governing verb; the beginning raises subject and predicate, an explanation al-Akhfash says is more analogical.
rows.anchor: والابتداء هو الذي رفع الخبر في قول بعضهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some grammarians say that the beginning raises both the subject and the predicate.
rows.anchor: فكذلك رفع الابتداء الاسم والخبر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other grammarians say that the predicate raises the subject; al-Akhfash accepts both accounts but prefers the first as more analogical.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: "رفع المبتدأ خبره"

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs put al-ḥamdu in the accusative as a verbal noun in place of the verb, equivalent to saying a praise to God or I praise with praise.
rows.anchor: وذلك ان اصل الكلام عنده على قوله

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs give al-ḥamdu a fixed kasra by treating it like indeclinable nouns; before and after are likewise fixed unless annexed, as the cited Qurʾanic examples show.
rows.anchor: فكسره، وذلك أنه جعله بمنزلة الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash cites a rajaz couplet about every living being meeting death and every pair ending in separation, then says this usage is scarcely known; the witnessed word is ithnayn.
rows.anchor: يا نفس صبرا كل حي لاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām makes li-llāh genitive, and rabb al-ʿālamīn al-raḥmān al-raḥīm is also genitive as an attribute of Allāh.
rows.anchor: جر باللام كما انجر قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open nūn in the sound masculine plural is an added marker that disappears in the singular; its fatḥa distinguishes it from the dual's always-kasra nūn.
rows.anchor: وأما فتح نون {العالمين} فانها نون جماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sound masculine plurals use wāw for nominative and yāʾ for accusative and genitive, while the dual uses alif for nominative and yāʾ for the other two cases.
rows.anchor: وجعلت الياء للنصب والجر نحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural nūn falls in annexation like the dual nūn; unlike the root nūn in broken plurals such as shayāṭīn, dahāqīn, and masākīn, which remains.
rows.anchor: وهذه النون تسقط في الاضافة كما تسقط نون الاثنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ladhīna has an added open nūn because it disappears in singular alladhī; the text also cites the nominative form alladhūn.
rows.anchor: فتسقط النون لانها زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Māliki yawm al-dīn is genitive because it is an attribute of Allāh.
rows.anchor: فانه يجر لانه من صفة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some read mālika in the accusative as a supplication; al-Akhfash says both accusative and genitive are permissible.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأها قوم {مالك} نصب على الدعاء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Other readers have malik without the long alif; al-Akhfash distinguishes this noun from mālik, the active participle from malaka, as qāhir is from qahara.
rows.anchor: اسم ليس بمشتق من فعل نحو قولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to addressing God as iyyāka is by revelation: God instructs the Prophet to say the praise and then to say iyyāka naʿbudu.
rows.anchor: فانما هذا على الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyāka is used instead of anta because the pronoun is an object of naʿbudu; object position takes ka, hi, or the iyyā form.
rows.anchor: لان هذا موضع نصب. واذا لم يقدر في موضع النصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyāka in both naʿbudu and nastaʿīn is accusative as the object; nominative positions instead take forms such as anta, antum, huwa, or hiya.
rows.anchor: اذا كان موضع رفع جعلت فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ihdinā means ʿarrifnā, make us know; the people of the Hijaz say hadaytuhu al-ṭarīq or the house, while other Arabs add ilā.
rows.anchor: فيقول: "عرفنا". واهل الحجاز يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim is accusative as an appositive to al-ṣirāṭ.
rows.anchor: أنعمت عليهم} نصب على البدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif in anʿamta is hamzat qaṭʿ because its imperfect is yanʿimu, with a ḍamma on the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: لانك تقول "ينعم" فالياء مضمومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr al-maghḍūbi can be an adjective for those blessed, though ghayr and mithl are ordinarily used with indefinites and can modify definite forms that carry an indefinite sense.
rows.anchor: قد احتيج اليهما في هذا الموضع فأجريتا صفة لما فيه الالف واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apposition is better than the adjective analysis because alladhī and alladhīna remain definite; he argues that rajul mithluka is generic, while Zayd mithluka only works as apposition.
rows.anchor: أجود من الصفة، لان "الذي" و "الذين" لا تفارقهما الالف واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣirāṭ has both sīn and ṣād forms; al-Akhfash prefers ṣād because that is how it is written throughout the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: الا انا نختار الصاد لان كتابها على ذلك في جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Arab usage can put al-jammāʾ al-ghafīr in the accusative despite its article, treating it like an indefinite expression.
rows.anchor: وقد قال العرب "هم فيها الجماء الغفير" فنصبوا

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some readers construe ghayr al-maghḍūbi as an exception outside the initial statement.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأ قوم {غير المغضوب عليهم} جعلوه على الاستثناء

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز
rows.claim: In the Hijaz dialect, an exception outside the initial statement after negation is accusative, as in mā fīhā aḥadun illā ḥimāran.
rows.anchor: في لغة أهل الحجاز فانه ينصب

rows.speaker: غيرهم
rows.claim: Other Arabs treat the exception as part of the initial statement and put it in the nominative.
rows.anchor: وغيرهم يقول: "هذا بمنزلة ما هو من الأول" فيرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A genitive form is explained by analogy to alladhī bi-l-rajul; al-Akhfash finds the adjective analysis weak and apposition better, as in the naṣiya example.
rows.anchor: وليس هو على الصفة بحسن ولكن على البدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr may alternatively be accusative as a circumstantial expression because it is indefinite while its antecedent is definite.
rows.anchor: نصبا على الحال لانها نكرة والأول معرفة

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs say hiyyāka for iyyāka, treating the initial alif as h, like ih or hih and haraqtu for araqtu.
rows.anchor: ومن العرب من يقول: "هياك" بالهاء

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز
rows.claim: The Hijaz dialect feminizes ṣirāṭ like al-ṭarīq, al-zuqāq, al-sabīl, al-sūq, and al-kalāʾ; Tamīm uses masculine forms, while Asad feminizes al-hudā.
rows.anchor: وأهل الحجاز يؤنثون "الصراط" كما يؤنثون "الطريق"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lāghiya means an idle word; the feminine form names the utterance by the pattern used for a horse-owner, armor-wearer, or poet.
rows.anchor: أي: لا تسمع كلمة لغو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses lābin and tāmir for someone possessing milk and dates, supporting this possessive pattern.
rows.anchor: أغررتني وزعمت أنك لابن بالصيف تامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular of namāriq, cushions, is nimriqa.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes Iram as the name of ʿĀd; others construe ʿĀd Iram as an annexation, naming either their father or, uncertainly, a town.
rows.anchor: فجعل {إرم} اسمه وبعضهم يقول {بعاد إرم} فاضافه الى {إرم}

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain qadara as having the same meaning as qattara, to constrict provision.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم {قدر} مثل {قتر}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the doubled form qaddara, al-Akhfash says God gives provision according to a measure.
rows.anchor: واما {قدر} فيقول: يعطيه بالقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic has paired forms ḥill/ḥalāl and ḥurum/ḥarām for the state of being permitted or resident; among the verb forms, ḥalalnā is preferred.
rows.anchor: فمن العرب من يقول "أنت حل" و"أنت حلال"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-lā iqtahama means he did not scale the obstacle, just as fa-lā ṣaddaqa means he did not believe.
rows.anchor: كما قال {فلا صدق} أي: فلم يصدق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash rejects an alternative construal and prefers the direct fakk raqaba phrase as the good reading.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا بذاك و {فك رقبة} هو الجيد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some gave a different syntactic construal of fakk raqaba in relation to the obstacle and the following or feeding phrase.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم {فك رقبة} وليس هذا بذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative yatīman is governed by iṭʿām, feeding.
rows.anchor: نصب "اليتيم" على "الإطعام"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā in wa-nafsin wa-mā sawwāhā means the One who fashioned it; God swears by Himself as Lord of the soul He formed, and the oath's answer is qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā.
rows.anchor: فاقسم الله تبارك وتعالى بنفسه وانه رب النفس التي سواها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāqat Allāh means God's she-camel, followed by the warning to beware harming her.
rows.anchor: أي: ناقة الله فاحذروا أذاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular of Sīnīn is Sīnīna.
rows.anchor: قال {وطور سينين} وواحدها "السينينة"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In mā yukadhdhibuka baʿdu bi-l-dīn, mā can refer to a human being; Arabic mā jāʾanī Zayd can mean alladhī jāʾanī Zayd.
rows.anchor: فجعل {ما} للانسان. وفي هذا القول يجوز "ما جاءني زيد" في معنى "الذي جاءني زيد"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salāmun hiya means she is safe or secure, that is, musallama.
rows.anchor: أي: هي سلام، يريد: مسلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maṭlaʿ al-fajr means the rising of dawn; here the verbal noun is formed only on mafʿal.
rows.anchor: والمصدر ها هنا لا يبنى الا على "مفعل"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second arāʾayta clause in verse 13 is appositional to the first in verse 11, and the predicate is the statement in verse 14 that God sees.
rows.anchor: وجعل الخبر {ألم يعلم بأن الله يرى}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nādīhi means his clan, since they are the people of the gathering place; al-nādī itself is the place and meeting council.
rows.anchor: ها هنا عشيرته وانما هم اهل النادي والنادي مكانه ومجلسه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some give zabānī as the singular of zabāniya.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: واحدها "الزباني"

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another says its singular is al-zābin, which al-Akhfash says he heard from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: "الزابن" سمعت "الزابن" من عيسى بن عمر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further reported singular is zabaniya.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم "الزبنية"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabs scarcely know a singular, he treats zabāniya as a plural with no singular like abābīl, indicating multitude like ʿabādīd and shaʿārīr.
rows.anchor: والعرب لا تكاد تعرف هذا وتجعله من الجمع الذي لا واحد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awḥā lahā means awḥā ilayhā, He revealed to it.
rows.anchor: قال {بأن ربك أوحى لها} أي: أوحى إليها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A variant uses ṣād in fa-waṣaṭna, while some read the sīn form fa-wasaṭna.
rows.anchor: قال {فوصطن به} وقال بعضهم {فوسطن}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular of ʿihn, wool, is ʿihana.
rows.anchor: وواحدها: "العهنة" مثل: "الصوف" و"الصوفة"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ in mā hiyah is a pause marker at the end of an āya.
rows.anchor: فلأن السكت عليها بالهاء لأنها رأس آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Li-īlāfi Quraysh means God did this so Quraysh would become accustomed; īlāfihim is an explanatory apposition and derives from ألف.
rows.anchor: فعل ذلك لايلاف قريش لتألف ثم ابدل فقال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some instead derive the form li-īlāf from the verb ālafū.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم {لإيلاف} جعلها من "آلفوا"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arāʾayta is read with or without the hamza; both are dialect forms, and frequent use of the word leads to hamza deletion.
rows.anchor: تحذف الهمزة لكثرة استعمال هذه الكلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaduʿʿu al-yatīm means he pushes the orphan away from his right; the verb is daʿaʿtuhu, adaʿʿu.
rows.anchor: يقول: "يدفعه عن حقه" تقول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shāniʾak is the one who hates you, from shaniʾtuhu, ashnaʾuhu, shanaʾan.
rows.anchor: تقول: "شنئته" ف"أنا أشنؤه" شنآنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because lā functions like mā, the clauses with lā aʿbudu and wa-lā antum ʿābidūn are nominative predicates of an initial subject.
rows.anchor: لأن {لا} تجري مجرى {ما} فرفعت على خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular of afwājan is fawj.
rows.anchor: في دين الله أفواجا} واحدهم: الفوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdi rabbika means that glorification should be joined to praise: tasbīḥ is remembrance, praising God for the conquest and other gifts; a person also says he has completed his portion of remembrance.
rows.anchor: على ما اعطيتك من فتح مكة وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabbat has the feminine tāʾ form that al-Akhfash calls jazm, as in ḍaraba/ḍarabat; tabba is an open-vowel masculine past verb.
rows.anchor: جزم لأن تاء المؤنث اذا كانت في الفعل فهو جزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He understands ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab as a description of the wife under an implied taṣlā, she will enter the Fire carrying wood.
rows.anchor: يقول: "وتصلى امرأته حمالة الحطب"

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some put ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab in the accusative as blame.
rows.anchor: ونصب بعضهم {حمالة الحطب} على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash also allows it as an indefinite circumstantial accusative with implied tanwīn, governed by taṣlā.
rows.anchor: ويجوز ان تكون {حمالة الحطب} نكرة نوى بها التنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥad is an appositive to Allāh, equivalent to saying huwa aḥad; some Arabs omit nunation to avoid two adjacent sukūns.
rows.anchor: فان قوله {أحد} بدل من قوله {الله}

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs omit nunation on aḥad to avoid the meeting of two sukūns.
rows.anchor: ومن العرب من لا ينون، يحذف لاجتماع الساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In wa-lam yakun lahu kufuwan aḥad, aḥad is the subject noun and kufuwan is its predicate.
rows.anchor: {أحد} هو الاسم و {كفوا} هو الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāsiq comes from ghasaqa/yaghsuqu and means darkness; waqaba/yaqibu means to enter into something.
rows.anchor: وهي: "الظلمة". و"وقب" "يقب" "وقوبا" وهو الدخول في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage gives malik with mīm ḍamma and mālik/malik forms with fatḥa or kasra; the ḍamma is also reported as a dialect for this meaning.
rows.anchor: وزعموا ان ضم الميم لغة في هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilāh al-nās is an appositive to malik al-nās.
rows.anchor: وقوله {اله الناس} بدل من {ملك الناس}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min al-jinnati wa-l-nās means protection from the evil whisperer among jinn and people; al-jinna means the jinn.
rows.anchor: يريد: "من شر الوسواس من الجنة والناس". و"الجنة" هم: الجن
